h: Gospels, notebooks and a giant bronze Newton
p: Before you even step inside, you'll meet Sir Isaac Newton. A huge bronze sculpture by Eduardo Paolozzi, based on a famous William Blake print, sits in the piazza, showing Newton hunched over measuring the universe with a pair of dividers. It's a great spot to sit with a coffee, and the red-brick building behind it, opened in 1997 and designed by Colin St John Wilson, is now Grade I listed.

The Treasures Gallery is a real who's who of the written word. Look out for the Lindisfarne Gospels, created on Holy Island in the early 700s, with intricate decoration that seems impossible for a human hand. Leonardo da Vinci's notebook pages, full of mirror-writing and sketches, are another favourite, as is the Codex Sinaiticus, one of the earliest surviving copies of the Christian Bible. Jane Austen fans can see her small portable writing desk, which feels surprisingly personal.

Many people don't realise you can apply for a free Reader Pass if you have a genuine research reason, which opens up the reading rooms and their millions of items. For a casual visit, though, the public spaces, the gallery and the regular talks and events are more than enough. An hour or two will cover the highlights nicely.

The library sits beside the Francis Crick Institute, a huge biomedical research centre, and a little further up the road at King's Cross, Granary Square's fountains are a favourite with kids on warm days. If you're a Harry Potter fan, Platform 9 3/4 at King's Cross station is just across the road.
